messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Amara is a twenty-year-old pharmacist who came to the United States with her family when she was twelve, but three years ago she returned to her country of origin for what was supposed to be a short visit. During that trip she was detained by armed men who accused her family of supporting opposition groups. For several days they kept her in a small concrete room with no windows. At various points they forced her head into a barrel of water until she lost consciousness, then dragged her back onto the floor, coughing and gasping. They screamed at her—endless arguments about things she did not know, demands she could not answer—and when she failed to give them what they wanted, they grabbed her wrists and made her kneel for hours, her arms twisted behind her back until her shoulders burned. She remembers fragments: the smell of mildew, the sound of a door sliding open, the weight of a hand on her neck. But whole sections of those days are missing, as though someone cut pieces out of a film. When she tries to tell her partner about it, the words vanish; she can only shake her head.

Now Amara works twelve-hour shifts at a chain pharmacy in a busy strip mall. Every morning she walks through the automatic doors and checks the layout for exits—the stockroom door, the employee bathroom window, the back delivery entrance. She never sits with her back to the store. When a customer raises their voice over a copay or a delayed prescription, Amara feels her chest lock and her palms go cold; she has to excuse herself to the break room, where she stands with her hands on the sink, watching the water run. She has stopped filling prescriptions that require her to draw up liquid from a vial because the motion of the syringe plunger makes her body stiffen, her shoulders hunch, her knees press together—the same position she held on that concrete floor, waiting for the next dunk.

She is in a relationship, and she loves her partner, but when they argue—even about something small, like forgetting to take out the trash—Amara’s mind goes blank and she hears only the raised voices from the room where she was held. She does not tell her partner this. She does not tell anyone. She is certain that if she starts thinking about what happened, the whole memory will flood her and she will not be able to function. So she pushes it down, keeps herself busy, works double shifts when she can. But at night, when she is alone in bed, she cannot let herself fall asleep. She lies alert, listening to the furnace click on, the floorboards settle, her own heartbeat. She keeps the bedroom door open so she can hear the front door. She has to know she can get out.

Over the months this vigilance has worn her down. She has started to believe she deserves to feel this way. Other people in that room did not survive, and she does not understand why she did. She tells herself, silently, that the exhaustion and the fear are exactly what she should carry. When she sees someone on the street who resembles one of the men—same height, same jacket, same way of walking—she crosses the street or ducks into a shop. She has stopped going to the park near her apartment because there is a large decorative pond, and even the sight of still water makes her stomach turn.

What finally brought Amara to the clinic was a moment at work last week. A teenager dropped a full cup of soda near the register; the liquid spread across the tile and Amara froze, her body locking into that old posture, her hands numb. A coworker touched her shoulder and she flinched so hard she knocked over a display. She could not explain herself. She went home early and cried for an hour, then called a number her partner had left on the kitchen counter weeks ago. She is afraid that telling the story will break something open inside her and she will never get it closed again. But she is also afraid of how small her life has become—how many places she avoids, how many arguments she walks away from, how tired she is of scanning every room before she can breathe.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Avoid Dreams: The vignette does not mention avoiding situations or times of day that bring on nightmares. It describes avoidance of triggers like water and arguments, and sleep vigilance, but not specifically avoidance of dreams or nightmare-inducing contexts.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.
